nodes.name: Cyclic Voltammetry Nanocavity Formation
nodes.procedure: The pristine Cu foil was treated with cyclic voltammetry in 0.1 M CO₂-saturated KHCO₃ solution. During the CV treatment, the Cu foil could be oxidized in the positive scan and reduced in the negative scan, creating nanocavities on the surface. The nanocavities became increasingly denser as the CV cycles increased, with changes occurring only at a depth of hundreds of nanometers.

nodes.characterization_summary: Pristine Cu foil shows smooth surface; 10-cycle Cu foil shows rough cratered morphology with nanocavities.
nodes.evidence_snippet: SEM image of the pristine Cu foil. (C) SEM image of the Cu foil treated with 10 CV cycles. (D) SEM image of the nanocavity marked with red circle in panel C.

nodes.characterization_summary: ECSA of 10-cycle Cu foil is 9 times larger than pristine Cu foil determined by double-layer capacitance measurement using Δj vs scan rate slopes.
nodes.evidence_snippet: It was clearly shown that the ECSA of the 10-cycle Cu foil was 9 times larger than that of the pristine Cu foil as presented by the slopes in Figure 3A.

nodes.characterization_summary: Pristine Cu foil shows Cu(OH) adsorption peak at ~0.484 V vs RHE on Cu(111) facets; 10-cycle Cu foil shows additional sharp peak at ~0.364 V vs RHE corresponding to (100) facets.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As displayed in Figure 3B, the pristine Cu foil showed an adsorption peak at ∼0.484 V versus RHE principally, which could be assigned to the Cu(OH) adsorption peak on Cu(111) facets. In contrast, the 10-cycle Cu foil showed an additional sharp peak appearing at ∼0.364 V versus RHE, which corresponded to (100) facets.

nodes.characterization_summary: 10-cycle Cu foil cross-section shows 0.208 nm interplanar distance matching d111 planes and 0.181 nm matching d200 planes.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The results demonstrated that there were two plane spacings of 0.208 and 0.181 nm on the 10-cycle Cu foil, corresponding to d111 and d200 planes, respectively (Figure 3D,E).

nodes.characterization_summary: No obvious diffraction peaks of Cu2O/CuO observed, demonstrating lack of long-range ordered crystalline oxide phases.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Xray diffraction (XRD) patterns showed that there were no obvious diffraction peaks of Cu2O/CuO (Figure S12), which demonstrated the lack of long-range ordered crystalline phases of oxide on the surface.

nodes.characterization_summary: 10-cycle Cu foil shows stronger CO* adsorption peak at ~2110 cm⁻¹ and new peaks at 1412, 1254, 1358, 1215 cm⁻¹ assigned to OCCOH* and OCCHO* intermediates.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Figures 4C and S22, there were two common peaks appearing at ∼2110 cm⁻¹ and ∼1630 cm⁻¹ on the pristine Cu foil and the 10-cycle Cu foil, which could be assigned to CO* species and COOH* species... Most importantly, there were four new peaks that only appeared on the 10-cycle Cu foil in the range from ∼1200 cm⁻¹ to ∼1450 cm⁻¹.

nodes.characterization_summary: Synchrotron-radiation XANES reveals active species on 10-cycle Cu foil are metallic Cu⁰ rather than Cu₂O.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Interestingly, synchrotron-radiation X-ray absorption near-edge spectroscopy (XANES) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) of Cu foils etched by Ar+ for different times (Figures S18 and S19) revealed that the active species on the 10-cycle Cu foil for CO2RR were metallic Cu⁰ rather than Cu₂O.

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS of Ar+ etched Cu foils confirms metallic Cu⁰ as active species on 10-cycle Cu foil.
nodes.evidence_snippet: synchrotron-radiation X-ray absorption near-edge spectroscopy (XANES) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) of Cu foils etched by Ar+ for different times (Figures S18 and S19) revealed that the active species on the 10-cycle Cu foil for CO2RR were metallic Cu⁰ rather than Cu₂O.

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ Raman spectra verify metallic Cu⁰ as active species on 10-cycle Cu foil.
nodes.evidence_snippet: This conclusion could be further verified by the in situ Raman spectra of the 10-cycle Cu foil (Figure S20).
